passage: So, I'm Akash. Dhruv and I had been married three years, and everyone kept asking when we'd have a baby. My mother, his aunts, even the neighbour. I realised we'd never actually talked about it properly. So one weekend we took a notebook to the park. Big questions: are we ready financially? Who takes leave? How do we want to discipline a child, without hitting like our parents did? We didn't agree on everything. Dhruv assumed I'd take all the leave. I didn't. That was a tense afternoon. But we worked out that he'd take time off too, and that we'd save for a year first. We aren't in a hurry now. It feels like our decision, not everyone else's.

qa.q: Where did Akash and Dhruv take their notebook?
qa.a: They took it to the park.

qa.q: Why was that afternoon tense for Akash?
qa.a: Dhruv assumed Akash would take all the leave, and Akash disagreed, which exposed an unspoken expectation.

qa.q: What made their conversation a good step toward parenthood?
qa.a: They discussed money, leave and parenting values openly, and agreed on shared care and a savings plan.

qa.q: How might their families see the couple's decision to wait a year?
qa.a: The relatives who kept asking may feel impatient, but the couple now has clear reasons of their own.

grounding: Shows a couple reflecting on readiness, finances, parenting values and sharing care before having a child.

passage: I'm Arnab, Pooja's colleague and friend. Pooja and her husband were thinking about having a baby. At lunch she'd bring printouts: childcare costs, leave policies from both their companies. At first I teased her about making a spreadsheet for a baby. She didn't laugh. She said she'd seen her mother give up work and never get it back, and she wanted to decide on purpose. One day she was upset because her husband's company offered almost no paternity leave. She seemed worried he wouldn't be involved. A few weeks later she said they'd agreed he'd use his holiday days and she'd return part-time. I don't know how they'll manage in the end. But I stopped teasing her.

qa.q: What did Pooja bring to lunch?
qa.a: She brought printouts of childcare costs and leave policies.

qa.q: Why did Pooja want to decide about parenthood so carefully?
qa.a: She had seen her mother give up work and never get it back, and she feared the same thing happening to her.

qa.q: How could a friend like Arnab better support Pooja?
qa.a: By listening and taking her planning seriously instead of teasing her about it.

qa.q: Why did Arnab stop teasing Pooja?

passage:
Day one: Mahima's sister arrived with her six-month-old for a weekend. Darshan held the baby for five minutes and handed her back when she cried. "We're definitely ready," he joked. Mahima wasn't laughing.

Day two: The baby woke four times. Mahima noticed she did every waking while Darshan slept. She said nothing, but made a note.

Two weeks later: At dinner Mahima brought it up. "If we have a child, will you get up at night too?" Darshan was quiet, then admitted he'd assumed she'd do more. "I don't want that," he said slowly. "I just never thought about it." They agreed to learn more first, from friends with babies, before deciding anything.

qa.q: How many times did the baby wake on day two?
qa.a: The baby woke four times.

qa.q: Why wasn't Mahima laughing at Darshan's joke?
qa.a: She sensed he wasn't taking the reality of caring for a baby seriously, which worried her.

qa.q: What step did the couple agree on before deciding?
qa.a: To learn more from friends with babies before making any decision about children.

qa.q: How might Darshan's view change after the conversation?
qa.a: He realised he'd assumed Mahima would do more, and he started thinking seriously about sharing care.

grounding: Shows a couple, over a few weeks, reflecting on readiness and equal sharing of care before parenthood.

passage: Zeenat, you ask how I knew I was ready for a baby. Your Tanuja Maasi will be honest: I didn't, fully. Nobody does. But at twenty-four, before we tried, your uncle and I did something my friends found strange: we sat down with a notebook for a month of Sundays. Money first: could we manage if I took a year off? Barely, so we dropped the plan for a second scooter. Then values. He wanted strict discipline, the way he was raised. I didn't. We argued, then agreed: no hitting, ever, and we talk before any punishment. Then the practical part: who wakes at night, who stays home when the child is sick. He said, 'Half and half.' I made him write it down. When Riya came, he did the night feeds on alternate days, and yes, I showed him the notebook when he forgot. Readiness is not a feeling, beta. It's conversations.

qa.q: Which plan did Tanuja and her husband drop to manage money?
qa.a: The plan to buy a second scooter.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel about her readiness before trying for a baby?
qa.a: Unsure; she admits she did not fully know, which is why she wanted to talk everything through first.

qa.q: What topics did Tanuja and her husband cover, and why does that matter?
qa.a: Money, parenting values like no hitting, and sharing night and sick-day care, so they began parenthood with agreements instead of assumptions.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's husband have felt when she showed him the notebook?
qa.a: Perhaps a bit sheepish, but reminded of his own promise, which kept the care shared.

grounding: An aunt recalls preparing for parenthood by talking through money, values and equal sharing of care.

passage: Hansa was four months pregnant when Santosh's factory in Rajkot switched him to rotating night shifts. Their savings were thin, and her mother lived three hundred kilometres away. One Sunday, over dal-bhaat, Hansa said, 'I don't want to be the only one who knows how to bathe the baby.' Santosh went quiet, then admitted he was scared he wouldn't know how. They made a plan on the back of a calendar. He would ask his supervisor for day shifts for the first two months, even at lower pay. He would join her antenatal classes at the government hospital on his days off. They would manage the budget by skipping the new TV. And they talked about what kind of parents they wanted to be: less shouting than they had grown up with. The supervisor gave him six weeks of day shifts, not eight. Not perfect. Santosh circled the date anyway.

qa.q: Where did Santosh plan to attend classes with Hansa?
qa.a: Antenatal classes at the government hospital, on his days off.

qa.q: Why did Santosh go quiet when Hansa spoke about bathing the baby?
qa.a: He was scared he would not know how to care for the baby, which he then admitted.

qa.q: How did they prepare despite thin savings and night shifts?
qa.a: By asking for day shifts, attending classes together, skipping a purchase to manage money, and agreeing on the kind of parents they wanted to be.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Santosh admitted his fear?
qa.a: Relieved that he was honest and willing to learn, which made sharing the care feel possible.

grounding: Shows an expecting couple preparing for parenthood under shift-work and money constraints while planning to share care.

passage: Tanvir's mother had started leaving baby-name books on the dining table of their Salt Lake flat. Ankita noticed and said nothing for a week. Then one Sunday she set down two cups of tea and a notebook. "Before your mother names our imaginary child, can we talk ourselves?" Tanvir laughed, then didn't. They made three columns: ready, not ready, don't know. Ready: they wanted a child, and their marriage felt steady. Not ready: Ankita's company gave six months' leave, Tanvir's gave two weeks. Don't know: whether they could afford the crèche near her office. "If I get two weeks, you'll end up doing everything," Tanvir said slowly. "And I'll resent it," Ankita said. So they made a plan. Tanvir would ask HR about longer leave; they would visit the crèche; and they would talk to a financial planner. "Six months," Tanvir said. "Then we decide. Us."

qa.q: How much leave does Tanvir's company give?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling during the week she said nothing?
qa.a: Ankita was probably irritated and uneasy at the pressure, wanting the decision to be their own.

qa.q: What made their three-column talk a useful way to prepare?
qa.a: It separated what they knew from what they didn't, exposed the leave gap that would make care unequal, and led to concrete steps.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's mother react to 'Then we decide. Us'?
qa.a: She might feel a bit left out, but also reassured that they are thinking seriously about a child.

grounding: A married couple in Kolkata calmly assess their readiness for a child, including leave, costs and sharing care equally.

passage:
"How did you know you were ready?" Jasleen asked, rocking Arohi's three-month-old while Arohi finally ate.
Arohi snorted. "I didn't. Nobody does."
"Then how did you decide?"
"We asked ourselves boring questions. Can we manage a year on less money? Who gets up at 3 a.m.? What do we do if we disagree about smacking, screens, God?"
"And?"
"Vikram and I disagreed about half of it." Arohi grinned. "We fought for a month. Then we wrote down what we agreed on. Night feeds split. No hitting, ever. Grandparents advise, they don't decide."
Jasleen looked down at the sleeping baby. "Manpreet wants a baby next year. I'm not sure I want one at all."
"Then that's your first boring question." Arohi put down her plate. "Don't let anyone rush you. Not Manpreet. Not me."
The baby stirred, and Jasleen didn't hand her back.

qa.q: How old is Arohi's baby?
qa.a: Three months old.

qa.q: What might Jasleen be feeling about Manpreet wanting a baby next year?
qa.a: Jasleen feels unsure and torn, not certain about wanting a child at all.

qa.q: Which of Arohi's 'boring questions' are most useful for Jasleen, and why?
qa.a: The questions about money, night feeds and parenting values, because they turn a vague wish into concrete choices and show where partners disagree.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Jasleen's uncertainty?
qa.a: Arohi respects it, treats it as a valid first question, and warns against anyone rushing the decision.

grounding: Two friends talk about readiness for parenthood, shared care and values, and the right not to be rushed.

passage: When I found out I was pregnant, I, Gurleen, cried in the bathroom, half joy and half terror. Baljeet hugged me and immediately started talking about cots. I wanted to talk about us. Both our mothers had done everything alone while our fathers "helped". I didn't want our child to grow up seeing that. So one evening we sat with a notebook and divided the invisible jobs, not only the visible ones: who books vaccinations, who notices we're out of nappies, who stays home when the baby is sick. Baljeet was quiet a while, then said, "I didn't realise how much Mummy was carrying." We signed up for the hospital's parenting class together, and he asked his manager about paternity leave the next week. We also sat with a financial planner about the first year. Our daughter is four months old now. We still argue about nappies, but it's a fifty-fifty argument.

qa.q: Which class did Gurleen and Baljeet sign up for together?
qa.a: The hospital's parenting class.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling on finding out about the pregnancy?
qa.a: Gurleen felt both joy and terror, crying in the bathroom.

qa.q: Why was dividing the invisible jobs an important step?
qa.a: It made sure care would be truly shared, not just 'helped' with, by naming tasks like vaccinations and sick days that often fall on one parent.

qa.q: How did Baljeet come to see his own mother differently?
qa.a: Baljeet realised how much his Mummy had carried alone, which seemed to move him to share the load.

grounding: A young woman looks back on preparing for parenthood with her husband by planning equal care and getting support.

passage:
Workshop note — "Before Baby" evening, community health centre.

Joseph and his wife Meenal came to the second session. I noticed Joseph had brought a small notebook and wrote down every question the couples asked.

During the "who will do the night feeds" exercise, Meenal said she would be on leave for six months and could do them. Joseph put his pen down. "I'll take alternate nights," he said. "You'll need sleep too. And my office has two weeks of paternity leave. I'll ask for all of it." Meenal looked surprised, then pleased.

Later he asked me privately whether it was normal to feel scared about not being a good father. His own father, he said, was often away. I told him the worry itself shows he is thinking about it, and suggested they both talk to their doctor and join the new-parents group at the centre.

I've given them the next session's reading list.

— Bhupen, community health worker

qa.a: Joseph had brought a small notebook and wrote down every question the couples asked.

qa.q: What was Joseph worried about when he spoke to Bhupen privately?
qa.a: Joseph was anxious about not being a good father, because his own father was often away.

qa.q: How could Joseph and Meenal keep preparing together before the baby comes?
qa.a: They could keep planning how care will be shared, talk to their doctor, and join the new-parents group at the centre.

qa.q: What was it like for Meenal when Joseph offered alternate nights?
qa.a: Meenal was surprised and pleased, as she had expected to handle the night feeds alone.

passage:
Sunday

Asif asked again at breakfast: "So, next year? Baby?" He was smiling.

I said, "Let's talk properly first," and he looked a bit wounded.

So I wrote the list I'd been carrying in my head.
— Work: I'm up for promotion in June. Would I still want it with a newborn? Would he step back if I did?
— Care: when Asif says he'll "help", I get tense. I don't want help. I want half.
— Money: do we know what the first year actually costs? We've never sat down with it.
— Values: how would we handle discipline? His family shouts; mine goes silent. Neither feels great.
— Us: are we ready to be tired together without blaming each other?

Tonight I showed him. He was quiet for a long time, then said, "I didn't know 'help' sounded like that." He added one line to the list himself: "Ask my brother what he wishes he'd planned."

I think we're closer to ready than we were this morning. Not there yet.

— Preeti

qa.q: When is Preeti up for promotion?
qa.a: Preeti is up for promotion in June.

qa.q: Why does Preeti get tense when Asif says he will "help"?
qa.a: Preeti feels uneasy because "help" suggests the care will mainly fall on Preeti, when the wish is to share it equally.

qa.q: What makes Preeti's list a useful way to decide about readiness?
qa.a: It puts work, care, money, values and the relationship on paper so the couple can talk about each one honestly instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did Asif react to seeing the list?
qa.a: Asif was quiet for a long time, surprised at how "help" sounded, and then took part by adding his own question to the list.

grounding: A young adult reflects on readiness for parenthood, listing work, care, money and values, and discusses sharing care equally with a partner.

passage:
In their small town in Uttarakhand, every family function had the same question for Neelam and Sahil: "When is the good news?" They'd been married two years.
One evening, after Sahil's aunt asked it for the third time that day, Neelam walked out to the terrace. Sahil followed. "Do you want a child now?" he asked her quietly. "Not what they want. You."
She thought. "Someday, yes. But not while I'm finishing my B.Ed. And not if it means I do everything."
They talked late. They listed what they'd need: Neelam's degree done, enough savings to manage a few months on one income, Sahil's parents' help in principle but not as their main plan. Sahil promised he'd take leave from the shop in the first months.
They decided: after her exams, they'd talk again. The next time his aunt asked, Sahil said, "When we're ready. You'll be the first to know."

qa.q: How long had Neelam and Sahil been married?
qa.a: Two years.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when she walked out to the terrace?
qa.a: Neelam felt pressured and frustrated by the repeated questions from relatives.

qa.q: What made their discussion a thoughtful way to prepare for parenthood?
qa.a: They talked about their own wishes, timing, money and sharing care before deciding, rather than responding to family pressure.

qa.q: How might Sahil's aunt see his answer at the next function?
qa.a: Sahil's aunt might feel mildly rebuffed but understand the couple would decide for themselves.

passage:
In their small flat in Haifa, Yosef and Zeynep had a spreadsheet titled "Maybe baby". Zeynep had made it, Yosef had laughed at it, and then they'd both filled it in.
One tab was money: what they'd need, what leave each could take. Another was values: how they'd handle two religions at home, screen time, discipline. The third tab was "Who does what at 3 a.m.?"
That was where they got stuck. Yosef's job gave him only a few days' leave. Zeynep said, "Then I'll do all the night feeds. And I'll resent you."
Yosef was quiet. The next week he asked his manager about longer parental leave and part-time options. The answer was maybe.
It wasn't solved. But they'd agreed they wouldn't start trying until the 3 a.m. tab had both their names on it, equally.

qa.q: What was the spreadsheet titled?
qa.a: "Maybe baby".

qa.q: How did Zeynep feel about doing all the night feeds?
qa.a: Zeynep felt worried about ending up resentful if the care wasn't shared.

qa.q: What did Yosef do after the conversation, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Yosef asked his manager about longer parental leave and part-time options, because sharing care equally depends on practical changes, not just good intentions.

qa.q: How might Yosef's manager see his request?
qa.a: The manager might be surprised but could see that Yosef is planning seriously for family life.

passage:
The parenting-readiness workshop at the community health centre in Chandigarh was held on Sunday mornings. Jyoti came with her husband, Arvind, both twenty-six. The facilitator, Jasleen, asked couples to sit back to back and each write down how many night wake-ups they expected to handle.
Jyoti wrote "most". Arvind wrote "some". When they turned around and compared, they both laughed nervously.
Jasleen didn't lecture. She asked, "What would 'equal' look like in your home?" and handed them a chart: feeding, nappies, doctor visits, sick days, washing.
They filled it in slowly. Arvind realised he'd never thought about who'd stay home when the baby was sick. Jyoti realised she'd assumed it would be her.
On the way home, Arvind said, "I'm going to ask about the leave policy at work tomorrow." Jyoti held his hand the whole bus ride.

qa.q: Where was the parenting-readiness workshop held?
qa.a: At the community health centre in Chandigarh.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti and Arvind laugh nervously when they compared answers?
qa.a: They felt awkward and a bit anxious, seeing they had very different expectations about sharing night wake-ups.

qa.q: How did Jasleen's approach help the couple prepare?
qa.a: Jasleen asked what equal would look like and used a practical chart, so the couple discovered hidden assumptions themselves.

qa.q: How might Arvind feel after the workshop?
qa.a: Arvind may feel a bit shaken at how little he had thought about sick days, but motivated to take a real, equal share.

grounding: Shows a young couple at a workshop reflecting on readiness and on sharing parenting care equally.

passage:
Dear Sangeeta Akka,
You asked last week whether Karthik and I are "planning anything yet," and I laughed it off. Here's the real answer.
We've started talking about it properly, not just "someday." We sat down with our budget and a list: what we'd change at work, who takes leave when, which of us is up at night. Karthik said he'd take a full month off, not the three days his father took. I cried a little at that, happy tears mostly.
But I'm also scared. I watched you after Anu was born, doing everything while your in-laws told you what you were doing wrong. I don't want that. We want to raise a child who argues politely and helps in the kitchen, whether a boy or a girl.
We're not ready yet. Maybe in a year. Can I call on Sunday and ask the questions nobody else answers honestly?
Love,
Yamini

qa.q: How long did Karthik say he would take off?
qa.a: He said he would take a full month off.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Yamini describe?
qa.a: Yamini feels happy and moved by Karthik's promise, but scared of repeating Sangeeta's lonely, criticised time after Anu was born.

qa.q: What steps show Yamini and Karthik preparing wisely?
qa.a: They talked through budget, leave and night duty, agreed to share care, and plan to ask Sangeeta honest questions before deciding.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel reading Yamini's memory of her early days with Anu?
qa.a: Sangeeta might feel understood and a little sad, touched that her hard time is helping Yamini plan differently 🤍
